segments.title: Treaty tonnage and ships fitted for equipment they do not carry
segments.body: A hypothetical return to naval treaties raises a distinction between building hulls and equipping them. The prediction is that Britain would build ships up to the permitted size but leave some of their intended armament uninstalled. A cruiser-sized ship might consequently carry destroyer-level firepower, while retaining provision for a cruiser's weapons. Meeting a tonnage allowance would therefore say little by itself about the installed combat capability.

evidence.note: A hypothetical cruiser-sized hull carries destroyer-level armament while retaining provision for more weapons.

segments.summary: A modern treaty counterfactual imagines British ships reaching their tonnage limits while carrying less armament than their hulls were designed to accept.

segments.title: Could more effective shells have kept Seydlitz from returning home?
segments.body: The Greenboy-shell counterfactual turns on how little reserve buoyancy Seydlitz had left after Jutland. Some shells that struck her failed to explode. Given the damage she sustained, additional functioning shells are judged enough to have prevented her return. Her condition in a photograph after reaching harbor was already the result of efforts to lighten her, including removing gun barrels. That image cannot be treated as showing the full weight she carried while struggling home.

evidence.note: The Greenboy-shell prompt, unexploded hits, and Seydlitz's condition after material and gun barrels had been removed in harbor.

segments.summary: Seydlitz's severe damage supports the judgment that additional shells exploding at Jutland would have prevented her return.
segments.question: What difference would Greenboy shells have made at Jutland?
segments.answerShort: Seydlitz would not have made it home if more of the shells that struck her had exploded, given how badly damaged she already was.

segments.title: Why piracy persisted after Rome dominated the Mediterranean
segments.body: Rome lacked a standing navy to suppress piracy after the Punic Wars. Dominance of the Mediterranean had not produced a continuing naval force to control it.

evidence.note: Rome's lack of a standing navy explains the persistence of piracy after the Punic Wars.

segments.summary: Rome's dominance after the Punic Wars did not ensure that it maintained a navy to control piracy.
segments.question: Why had piracy grown when Rome controlled the Mediterranean after the Punic Wars?
segments.answerShort: Rome did not maintain a standing navy to suppress it.

segments.title: Ellwood as a visible coastal target
segments.body: The Ellwood oil field near Santa Barbara was an attractive target of opportunity because it was undefended, visibly industrial, and connected to major oil companies. Good communications meant that news of an attack could travel quickly. Drawing attention to an attack on the American mainland was central to the target's appeal. The raid came on February 23, 1942, as President Franklin D. Roosevelt was due to address the country by radio.

evidence.note: Ellwood's undefended oil facilities, major industrial connections, good communications, and the announced presidential speech made an attack likely to receive attention.

segments.summary: Ellwood's undefended oil facilities and good communications made it a conspicuous coastal target where an attack would quickly attract attention.

segments.title: Japan's thin submarine patrol off the West Coast
segments.body: I-17 belonged to the seven-submarine patrol sent toward the American West Coast during the Pearl Harbor operation. The boats probably sank two merchant ships, damaged six more, and twice encountered American air or surface forces. All seven returned to friendly waters, and some, including I-17, returned to American waters after resupplying at Kwajalein. A counterfactual alternative would divert resources from Yamato and Musashi toward carriers, cruisers, and more long-range submarines. Britain's initial wartime shift toward small vessels later created difficulties when the fall of Norway and France increased the need for larger ships. American construction emphasized battleships and carriers without a comparable investment in small Flower-class-scale escorts. The limited Japanese patrol and the American escort shortage both reflected choices about which ships to build.

evidence.note: Seven Japanese submarines patrolled the American West Coast, where a larger force of long-range boats could have caused greater disruption.
Seven Japanese submarines probably sank two merchant ships and damaged six off the American West Coast, exposing a shortage of small U.S. escorts despite extensive capital-ship construction.

segments.summary: Seven Japanese submarines produced real disruption off an enormous coastline, exposing the mismatch between American capital-ship construction and its shortage of small escorts.

segments.title: I-17 and Kozo Nishino
segments.body: I-17 was a large I-15-class submarine, displacing 3,713 tons submerged and measuring 111.4 meters long. It carried six 21-inch torpedo tubes, a 5.5-inch deck gun, and a Yokosuka E14Y seaplane. It appears to have carried 17 torpedoes, against a theoretical capacity of 18. A popular story makes Kozo Nishino a merchant captain who fell into a cactus and later returned to avenge oil workers' laughter. That identification conflicts with his career as a submarine officer, although another Japanese merchant mariner could have suffered the accident. Nishino was one of Japan's most accomplished submarine commanders.

evidence.note: I-17's dimensions, submerged displacement, six torpedo tubes, 17 torpedoes against a theoretical 18, and 5.5-inch gun.
The merchant-captain cactus story is rejected as incompatible with the experience required to command a submarine.
The torpedo-tube calibre is corrected to 21 inches, followed by the Yokosuka E14Y seaplane.
Nishino's career as a submarine officer and assessment as one of Japan's strongest submarine commanders.

segments.summary: I-17 combined torpedoes, a deck gun, and a seaplane under a career submarine commander whose background contradicts the popular revenge story.

segments.title: Why tankers also need escort ships
segments.body: Building a tanker is welcome, provided an escort is built with it. The objection concerns providing protection for the tanker alongside the additional hull.

evidence.note: Tanker construction is supported on condition that an escort ship is built alongside it.

segments.summary: A tanker-building proposal receives a simple condition: provide an escort with it.
segments.question: What is wrong with building a tanker?
segments.answerShort: Nothing, provided the fleet also builds an escort ship to protect it.

segments.title: What the Ellwood bombardment actually hit
segments.body: I-17 stopped opposite Ellwood at 19:00 on February 23, 1942, and opened fire fifteen minutes later at a Richfield aviation-fuel tank beyond the beach. The skeleton night crew initially mistook the explosions for an industrial mishap until a worker spotted the submarine. The low, wave-buffeted gun position and lack of a proper fire-control system made precise shooting difficult. Shells destroyed a derrick and pump house and caused minor damage to the pier and catwalks, while missing the fuel tanks. A deputy told a caller that aircraft were coming, but none arrived; night-qualified American pilots were scarce, with few available in California. Firing stopped at 19:35 after an estimated 12 to 25 shells, with roughly 25 judged more plausible for the time spent firing. The deliberate shore target distinguishes Ellwood from the incidental shells that fell at Orleans in 1918.

evidence.note: The 19:00 arrival, 19:15 opening fire on a Richfield aviation-fuel tank, and workers' initial confusion about the explosions.
The submarine's unstable low gun position, limited fire control, absent aircraft response, damaged structures, missed tanks, and 19:35 ceasefire.
Ellwood's deliberate shore bombardment is distinguished from incidental shelling at Orleans, before the comparison turns to invasion scares.

segments.summary: I-17 fired for twenty minutes at Ellwood's fuel installations, missing the tanks while damaging a derrick, pump house, and nearby structures.

segments.title: What I-17's 5.5-inch deck gun could do
segments.body: I-17's 5.5-inch 11th Year Type deck gun had a nominal five-round-per-minute firing rate, a muzzle velocity of 700 meters per second, and a maximum range of 16,000 meters. Its single mounting elevated to 30 degrees; the twin mounting's 40-degree elevation did not apply to I-17. Twenty minutes at the rated speed would yield 100 shots, well above contemporary estimates of 12 to 25 rounds at Ellwood. Roughly 25 is judged more plausible than either the lowest estimate or continuous maximum fire. The same gun had already sunk the tanker SS Emidio, while at Ellwood its shells missed the intended fuel tanks.

evidence.note: I-17's single 5.5-inch gun elevated to 30 degrees, was rated at five rounds per minute, and fired at 700 metres per second to a maximum range of 16,000 metres; those figures make roughly 25 shells more plausible than either 12 or the theoretical 100.
I-17 had already used the same deck gun to sink the tanker SS Emidio.

segments.summary: I-17's gun specifications put the Ellwood shell estimates in perspective: its theoretical rate of fire greatly exceeded the likely bombardment total.

segments.title: Ellwood and the Battle of Los Angeles
segments.body: No one died at Ellwood, but three deaths in traffic accidents and two deaths from heart attacks were associated with the Battle of Los Angeles the following night. A sincere but mistaken submarine sighting, an Office of Naval Intelligence warning, air-raid sirens, and a possible meteorological balloon all fed the alarm. The 37th Coast Artillery Brigade and other defenders fired more than 1,400 rounds at unconfirmed targets, while interceptor aircraft remained on the ground to avoid the anti-aircraft barrage. Fear, fragmented information, and poor coordination turned a materially minor coastal raid into a dangerous civil-defense crisis.

evidence.note: Ellwood caused no deaths, whereas the following night's Battle of Los Angeles was associated with fatal traffic accidents and heart attacks.
Reverend Arthur Basham of Montecito sincerely reported another submarine heading south and apparent shore signals, although I-17 had sailed west.

Confused alerts led to a blackout and mass anti-aircraft fire during the Battle of Los Angeles, causing property damage amid fatal traffic accidents and heart attacks without a confirmed enemy aircraft.
The probable meteorological balloon, the coordination failure around its launch, and the raid's intended psychological timing.

segments.summary: The Ellwood raid primed defenders for the Battle of Los Angeles, when confused warnings and mass anti-aircraft fire caused casualties without a confirmed enemy aircraft.

segments.title: Did the anti-aircraft fire hit the Los Angeles balloon?
segments.body: The balloon was inferred afterward from the meteorological unit's launch record rather than recovered as a confirmed target. There is no indication that the barrage hit it. Launching a weather balloon during a coastal alert suggests that air-defense and meteorological personnel were not sharing information effectively. Routine activity became dangerous because the commands responsible for the same airspace failed to coordinate.

evidence.note: The presumed balloon was traced to a 1 a.m. meteorological launch, raising questions about coordination during the alert.

segments.summary: The proposed weather-balloon explanation depends on a launch discovered afterward, with no indication that the barrage hit it.
segments.question: Did defenders actually hit the meteorological balloon associated with the Battle of Los Angeles?
segments.answerShort: No. The balloon is a later probable explanation for the alert, but there is no indication that the anti-aircraft barrage hit it.

segments.title: Why Baltimore was defended differently from Washington
segments.body: The 4,250 British troops that burned Washington had faced 7,640 Americans, yet poor American leadership helped turn the action into a rout. Baltimore presented a different problem. Roughly 5,000 British troops met a defense that could draw on about 27,000 militia and regulars, more than 100 guns around Hampstead Hill, and Fort McHenry's artillery. Experienced commanders and prepared positions made Baltimore a much harder target. The comparison gives Ellwood's later invasion scare a deeper historical reference point: the United States had experienced a capital burned and a major port threatened from the sea.

evidence.note: Unlike poorly led Washington, Baltimore could draw on about 27,000 militia and regulars, more than 100 guns around Hampstead Hill, and Fort McHenry's defences.

segments.summary: The contrast between the burning of Washington and the defense of Baltimore explains an older American memory of coastal attack and invasion.

segments.title: An uncertain staff-college wargame of the War of 1812
segments.body: Dr. Clarke recalls an Indian historian's story about a staff-college wargame held in Russia in the early 1980s. Indian participants played Britain and Russian participants played the Americans, with permission to alter historical conditions. The British side brought Wellesley and an additional 15,000 troops to North America. Experienced command and substantial reinforcements could have changed the fighting at Baltimore and New Orleans. Both the truth of the secondhand story and the reliability of the exercise remain uncertain.

evidence.note: Dr. Clarke's explicitly uncertain recollection of an Indian historian's staff-college wargame story, including Wellesley and 15,000 additional troops.

segments.summary: A secondhand wargame story changes British command and troop numbers to explore a different War of 1812.

segments.title: Britain's three-pronged campaign in 1814
segments.body: Baltimore was one of three simultaneous British operations aimed toward Baltimore, New York, and New Orleans, each originally expected to receive roughly 10,000 troops. The Baltimore force moved early after its easy success at Washington, while more veterans and heavier naval support became available as the European war wound down. Britain had also occupied much of Maine and proclaimed the colony of New Ireland, although it later returned the territory under the Treaty of Ghent. Possible ambitions to keep other ports remain uncertain, but expeditionary lift, veteran formations, and bargaining leverage made the campaign more than a single raid on one city. In a clearly counterfactual extension, British possession of major American ports could later have intersected with Britain's anti-slavery policy, creating political consequences beyond the immediate campaign.

evidence.note: The three British operations, their intended troop allocations, and the confidence created by Washington's capture.
Conditional British territorial ambitions, veteran reinforcements, and the additional naval support that the end of fighting in Europe could release.
The brigades sent toward Baltimore formed part of simultaneous British pressure on several ports, whose capture could have produced consequences well beyond a single coastal raid.

segments.summary: The Baltimore expedition belonged to a wider British attempt to pressure several American ports while veteran manpower and naval forces were becoming available after the Napoleonic Wars.

segments.title: North Point, Fort McHenry, and the British withdrawal
segments.body: Samuel Smith used the American force at North Point to delay the British advance while Baltimore's main defenses were completed. British commander Robert Ross was killed, although the identity of the man who shot him remains uncertain, and Arthur Brooke took over. The Americans withdrew to earthworks under Commodore John Rodgers, with naval personnel helping defend the redoubt. Fort McHenry kept British ships too far away to provide the close fire support needed against the stronger inner defenses. British troops adapted after a failed attack and overran positions on the American right, but Brooke chose bombardment and withdrawal over a costly frontal assault. His orders restricted an attack unless the defenders were far fewer than they proved to be. The large flag raised at Fort McHenry on September 14 was the normal morning flag, rather than a special gesture to taunt the British. The troops then sailed toward New Orleans; suggestions of further reinforcements, including Wellington, belong to a counterfactual continuation of the war.

evidence.note: North Point's delaying purpose, uncertainty over who killed Ross, the American withdrawal, and Commodore John Rodgers's earthworks.
The strength of the inner defenses and Fort McHenry's role in denying British naval fire support.
The routine morning flag raising, orders limiting an assault, the withdrawal toward New Orleans, and speculation about further reinforcements if the war continued.

segments.summary: American delaying action at North Point and Fort McHenry's denial of naval fire support made a direct assault on Baltimore too costly for the British plan.

segments.title: Wartime news and British support for continued fighting
segments.body: Slow news helped shape British perceptions of the war in North America. Reports arrived intermittently, and recent news included a succession of British victories. Many Britons also regarded the American attack as assistance to Napoleon. These circumstances support the argument that long years of warfare had not automatically exhausted public support for continued fighting.

evidence.note: Slow news, reported British victories, and contemporary hostility to perceived American assistance to Napoleon.

segments.summary: Intermittent news, reports of victories, and hostility to perceived support for Napoleon explain continued British support for the war.

segments.title: Checking the claim that Wellington visited Canada
segments.body: A claim that the Duke of Wellington visited Canada can be checked against the sequence of his post-Waterloo military, political, and diplomatic duties. No obvious period appears in which the voyage would fit, so the story remains doubtful, although the possibility is not ruled out. Canadian places bearing Wellington's name establish an association with his reputation, but they do not prove that he visited. A proposed visit has to fit the time needed to cross the Atlantic alongside those documented commitments.

evidence.note: Wellington's appointments and post-Waterloo negotiations leave no obvious opening for the proposed Canadian visit.
The warning that Canadian places named for Wellington do not by themselves establish a visit.

segments.summary: Wellington's post-Waterloo appointments leave no obvious time for a Canadian visit, despite local traditions associating his name with the country.

segments.title: Did Britons see the War of 1812 as a betrayal?
segments.body: The description of America supporting Napoleon reflected a belief sincerely held by many Britons. In that view, the United States had attacked while Britain was fighting a ruler they regarded as a scourge of Europe. Calling the belief mere propaganda would miss how seriously contemporaries took it.

evidence.note: A sincere British belief that America was helping Napoleon underlay the language of betrayal.

segments.summary: The language of American betrayal reflected a sincerely held British wartime perception.
segments.question: Was the claim that America stabbed Britain in the back by siding with Napoleon merely propaganda?
segments.answerShort: It also reflected a sincere British public view that the United States had attacked while Britain was fighting Napoleon, whom many Britons regarded as Europe's great enemy.

segments.title: U-156 and the 1918 action off Orleans
segments.body: U-156 attacked the tug Perth Amboy, its barges, and the schooner Lansford with gunfire, probably conserving scarce torpedoes against these slow targets. Perth Amboy was heavily damaged, while the schooner and three barges sank. Flying boats from the recently completed Naval Air Station Chatham dropped bombs that failed to explode, with inexperienced bomb-arming and loading personnel offered as the explanation. U-156 returned fire at the aircraft and sent shells into marshes and onto Orleans Beach. During the hour-long engagement, the submarine fired 147 rounds. A Coast Guard surf boat rescued 32 sailors without fatalities. Enemy shells reached American soil, but the shore was not the intended target, which distinguishes Orleans from Ellwood.

evidence.note: U-156 probably used its deck gun rather than scarce torpedoes against the slow tug Perth Amboy, its barges, and the schooner Lansford.
U-156 damaged the coastal vessels, exchanged ineffective fire with flying boats, accidentally sent shells ashore, and withdrew after a Coast Guard surf boat rescued 32 sailors.

segments.summary: During the Orleans action, a German U-boat attacked coastal traffic, exchanged fire with flying boats, and accidentally sent shells onto American soil.

segments.title: Why U-156 would conserve its torpedoes
segments.body: U-156's ammunition supply helps explain the likely choice of gunfire against slow coastal traffic. She carried 18 torpedoes, alongside 1,672 rounds for her 5.9-inch guns and 764 rounds for her 88 mm guns. Torpedoes were a much smaller resource to expend. Gunfire therefore offered a way to attack the tug and its tows while preserving torpedoes, although the explanation is an inference about the commander's choice.

evidence.note: The 18 torpedoes, 1,672 rounds for 5.9-inch guns, and 764 rounds for 88 mm guns support the inferred choice to conserve torpedoes.

segments.summary: U-156 carried far more gun ammunition than torpedoes, making gunfire a plausible choice against a slow tug and its tows.

segments.title: Did U-152's crew buy newspapers in Rhode Island?
segments.body: The Rhode Island anecdote is not established fact, and the submarine number may be wrong. The related U-151 class did have a documented commercial background, including Deutschland's unarmed cargo voyages between Germany and the United States. Photographs show Deutschland unloading at New London in 1916. Genuine blockade-running operations make the newspaper story plausible without proving its specific details.

evidence.note: Uncertainty over the Rhode Island story and submarine identity, followed by Deutschland's merchant voyages and photographs of unloading at New London in 1916.

segments.summary: The Rhode Island newspaper story remains uncertain, while Deutschland's commercial voyages provide firmer evidence of German submarine visits to America.
segments.question: Did U-152 visit Rhode Island closely enough for crewmen to go ashore and buy newspapers?
segments.answerShort: The story and submarine number remain uncertain, although that kind of bold visit was plausible for the large German cruiser-submarine family.

segments.title: The Peter Iredale wreck beside Fort Stevens
segments.body: The steel four-masted barque Peter Iredale was lost on the Oregon coast after a sixteen-year career. Thick mist, strong winds, and a rising tide drove the ballast-laden ship onto Clatsop Spit in October 1906, but a lifeboat from Hammond helped evacuate the crew without casualties. The inquiry commended the crew, while changing weather and the ship settling into the sand defeated plans to tow her free. Remnants of the wreck remain visible on the beach.

evidence.note: The Peter Iredale's construction, rig, voyage, and cargo state.
Grounding, lifeboat rescue, the inquiry's commendation of the crew, and the unsuccessful effort to refloat the ship.

segments.summary: The four-masted barque Peter Iredale links Fort Stevens to an earlier story of sail, grounding, rescue, and an unsuccessful salvage attempt.

segments.title: Fort Stevens and submarine gunfire limits
segments.body: I-25 followed fishing boats through the Columbia River approaches to avoid minefields and surfaced to attack Fort Stevens on June 21, 1942. The fort had heavy coastal artillery, including 12-inch mortars and disappearing guns, but its commander withheld fire because the submarine lay beyond effective range. Blackout concealed the target, while the submarine's motion and low firing position made accurate night shooting difficult. Its 17 shells mostly landed in a baseball diamond or swamp, with damaged telephone cables the only substantial result. An A-29 Hudson found the submarine, which evaded its bombs and submerged undamaged. The raid nevertheless prompted coastal barbed-wire defenses that entangled the nearby Peter Iredale wreck until the war ended.

evidence.note: I-25's approach, Fort Stevens' armament, the decision to withhold fire, and the difficulties of submarine gunnery at night.
The damaged telephone cables, 17-shell total, and unsuccessful A-29 Hudson attack on the departing submarine.
The bombardment intensified invasion fears and prompted barbed-wire defenses that entangled the Peter Iredale wreck.

segments.summary: The Japanese shelling of Fort Stevens produced far more alarm than military damage.

segments.title: Could the post-Napoleonic settlement reopen the Louisiana Purchase?
segments.body: Rumors held that Spain, other coalition powers, or even restored Bourbon France might join a continuing North American war to challenge Napoleon's sale of Louisiana. This was a possible diplomatic and military outcome rather than a settled plan. For France's restored monarchy, an expedition could also remove former Napoleonic soldiers from domestic politics by sending them far from France. The European peace settlement, colonial claims, and postwar demobilization could therefore have intersected with an unfinished American conflict.

evidence.note: Rumours of European intervention challenged the Louisiana Purchase, and a French expedition was one possible means of removing former Napoleonic soldiers from domestic politics.

segments.summary: Renewed European claims to the Louisiana Purchase were a speculative post-1814 possibility that linked diplomacy to the problem of demobilizing Napoleon's veterans.

segments.title: Were Fort Stevens' guns upgraded?
segments.body: The guns were eventually upgraded. No replacement weapon or date is specified.

evidence.note: A brief confirmation that the guns at Fort Stevens were eventually upgraded, without weapon or date details.

segments.summary: Fort Stevens' guns were eventually upgraded.
segments.question: Did they upgrade the guns at Fort Stevens?

segments.title: Why Japan occupied the Aleutian Islands
segments.body: The Aleutian Islands campaign turned an invasion scare into a real occupation of American territory, accompanied by Japanese attacks on Dutch Harbor. The operation could distract American attention during Midway, establish forward scouting positions after the Doolittle Raid exposed Japan's northern vulnerability, and deliver the psychological value of taking United States soil. Germany's occupation of the Channel Islands offered a comparison: possession carried symbolic value even when the territory offered limited direct strategic return. A colder hypothetical alternative would have been to mine the islands and force Britain to bear the supply problem without Germany maintaining a garrison. Both examples show that occupation decisions can serve prestige as well as operational needs.

evidence.note: Japan occupied Attu and Kiska during the Midway operation, gaining forward scouting bases after the Doolittle Raid exposed the northern approaches.

The Aleutian occupation protected Japan's northern approaches, diverted American attention, supplied scouting positions, and delivered the psychological effect of taking U.S. territory, so no single motive explains it.

segments.summary: The occupation of Attu and Kiska served several aims at once: protecting Japan's northern approaches, complicating the Midway campaign, and claiming American territory for psychological effect.

segments.title: Was the Aleutian campaign only a Midway diversion?
segments.body: A diversion was one purpose of the Aleutian operation. Extending Japan's northern perimeter gave it an independent military purpose as well. The carrier-lure explanation captures part of the plan, while a single-motive account leaves out the northern objective.

evidence.note: The carrier-lure explanation is considered alongside the northern perimeter objective and the operation's multiple purposes.

segments.summary: The Aleutian operation combined a diversionary role with a separate aim of extending Japan's defensive perimeter.
segments.question: Was Japan's Aleutian operation intended to lure American carriers north and draw the main Japanese fleet after them?
segments.answerShort: It had a diversionary role and also served Japan's effort to extend its defensive perimeter.

segments.title: Kinkaid's path from battleships to North Pacific command
segments.body: Thomas Kinkaid's early battleship service and ordnance engineering work preceded his carrier-war commands. After serving as naval attaché in Italy and Yugoslavia, he commanded cruisers protecting Lexington at Coral Sea and Hornet at Midway. He then led the Enterprise-centered Task Force 16 during the Solomon Islands campaign, including the Eastern Solomons and Santa Cruz. In January 1943 he took charge of the North Pacific Force and the recovery of the Aleutians. Promotion to vice admiral followed in June, and in November he became commander of the Seventh Fleet and Allied naval forces in the Southwest Pacific.

evidence.note: Kinkaid's battleship and ordnance background, carrier-related commands, North Pacific appointment, and later Seventh Fleet command.

segments.summary: Kinkaid brought battleship, ordnance, cruiser, and carrier-task-force experience to the recovery of the Aleutians.

segments.title: Hosogaya's withdrawal at the Komandorski Islands
segments.body: Boshiro Hosogaya was escorting transports to reinforce Kiska when an American force intercepted him near the Komandorski Islands in March 1943. His two heavy cruisers, two light cruisers, and four destroyers faced one American heavy cruiser, one light cruiser, and four destroyers. After USS Salt Lake City suffered severe damage, Hosogaya mistook colored shell splashes for an air attack and withdrew. Japanese higher command treated the retreat from an inferior surface force as cowardice and removed him from command. The argument in favor of his decision depends on what that apparent air attack implied: the visible American ships could have screened an unseen carrier force. Continuing against the known surface force offered a prospect of victory, while an attack by a larger force threatened cruisers Japan could ill afford to lose.

evidence.note: Boshiro Hosogaya withdrew from the Komandorski action after mistaking coloured shell splashes for an air attack, but preserving his cruiser force could still be rational if an unseen carrier threat seemed possible.

segments.summary: Hosogaya's apparent surface advantage at Komandorski competed with the possibility of an unseen American carrier force.

segments.title: The carrier raids on Dutch Harbor
segments.body: The Japanese carriers Ryujo and Junyo launched two raids against Dutch Harbor on June 3 and 4, 1942, despite limited work-up and difficult North Pacific conditions. Dutch Harbor was the closest substantial American base able to send troops and aircraft against the Aleutian landings, so suppressing it helped protect the small occupation force. Japanese aircraft hit barracks, fuel storage, the hospital, grounded aircraft, and ships, while American gun crews improvised a defense and fighters engaged the returning strike. Northwestern's size led attackers to mistake the beached transport for a warship, although it housed civilian workers. Firefighters saved its hull, and its power plant continued supplying steam and electricity ashore. A damaged Zero crash-landed on Akutan Island, killing its pilot while leaving the aircraft recoverable. American forces later repaired and examined it to learn the fighter's strengths and weaknesses. On June 5, Kakuta received orders to stop further attacks and head toward the Central Pacific after the defeat at Midway.

evidence.note: Ryujo and Junyo launched the first Dutch Harbor strike against improvised American defences, inflicting casualties when aircraft hit the barracks.
Dutch Harbor could rapidly support a response to the Aleutian landings, so the second raid struck its fuel, hospital, aircraft, barracks, and ships while both sides lost aircraft.
The Akutan Zero's recovery and the carrier force's withdrawal after Midway.

segments.summary: Two small Japanese carriers struck Dutch Harbor, damaged its facilities, and inadvertently gave the United States a recoverable Zero fighter for technical study.

segments.title: Ryujo, Junyo, and the limits of carrier readiness
segments.body: Ryujo's design tried to exploit the 10,000-ton treaty threshold, leaving Japan with a small carrier for the northern operation. Junyo was a merchant conversion purchased in 1941 and completed as a carrier in May 1942. Her completion only weeks before the June raids left little time to work up. The Dutch Harbor force therefore combined a small prewar carrier with a newly completed conversion whose preparation was still limited.

evidence.note: Ryujo's treaty-constrained size and Junyo's May 1942 completion left limitations in hull capacity and preparation time.

segments.summary: The Dutch Harbor carrier force combined Ryujo's small hull with Junyo's limited time to work up after conversion.

segments.title: Dutch Harbor's improvised ground defense
segments.body: Dutch Harbor received no specific warning before the first Japanese aircraft arrived, although its units had been on alert for days. Gun crews acted without direction from headquarters, using 3-inch and 37 mm guns, .50-caliber machine guns, and even small arms against aircraft flying low over the base. Bombs that hit two barracks killed 17 men from the 37th Infantry Regiment and eight from the 151st Engineers. During the night, the 206th moved guns from exposed mountain positions toward Unalaska and the harbor to prepare for an expected landing. Moving the guns also kept troops occupied and served as a deception by shifting firepower away from exposed prepared positions. Civilian contractors filled sandbags for the new positions, turning the interval between raids into a hurried local mobilization.

evidence.note: The lack of specific warning, the improvised anti-aircraft response, low-flying attackers, and the fatal barracks strikes.
The 206th moving guns overnight and civilian contractors filling sandbags for the new positions.

segments.summary: Gun crews, infantrymen, and civilian contractors improvised defenses during and between the two Japanese raids on Dutch Harbor.

segments.title: Aleutian supply lines and the unfinished Alaska Highway
segments.body: The Aleutian campaign began before the infrastructure needed to support it was fully developed. The Alaska Highway had received final authorization only in February 1942, a few months before the Japanese attacks. Much American support still had to come from Seattle. Long distances and the lack of established northern connections made infrastructure a constraint on the response.

evidence.note: The highway's February authorization and Seattle's role in supporting operations before northern infrastructure was established.

segments.summary: The Alaska Highway was newly authorized when the Aleutian campaign began, leaving American forces dependent on distant support.

segments.title: Kiska's weather station and William House's evasion
segments.body: Five hundred Japanese naval troops overwhelmed the American weather station on Kiska. Ten Americans were present at the twelve-person station: two were killed and seven captured, while Chief Petty Officer William House escaped. House survived on plants and worms for fifty days. Cold and starvation eventually forced him to surrender at a weight of about 80 pounds. The capture exposed how little resistance a small isolated weather detachment could offer to a landing force.

evidence.note: The Kiska landing, the tiny American weather-station force, and William House's fifty-day evasion.

segments.summary: Kiska's tiny weather-station detachment was overwhelmed, while William House evaded capture for fifty days before starvation forced his surrender.

segments.title: Was the Akutan Zero an advanced prototype?
segments.body: The captured aircraft was an improved Zero entering service. American investigators had not previously examined that newer variant so closely, so recovering it had substantial intelligence value. Whether examining it led to Hellcat improvements is left unresolved.

evidence.note: The Akutan aircraft is identified as an improved Zero entering service, rather than the advanced prototype suggested in the question.

segments.summary: The Akutan aircraft was an improved Zero with intelligence value because American investigators had not examined that generation so closely.
segments.question: Was the captured Akutan Zero an advanced prototype whose study led to improvements in the F6F Hellcat?
segments.answerShort: It was an improved Zero variant rather than an advanced prototype, but its recovery still revealed the newer variant's characteristics at close range.

segments.title: Could the Aleutians become an invasion route to Japan?
segments.body: Logistics mattered more than map distance alone. Operating east-to-west along the island chain would require ships, bases, supplies, and personnel able to endure severe currents, long distances, and extreme cold. The route was possible, but it was markedly less practical than the approaches the Allies chose.

evidence.note: Severe currents, distance, cold, and additional support requirements made an Aleutian advance much harder than the route actually chosen.

segments.summary: Severe currents, distance, cold, and supply requirements made an advance toward Japan through the Aleutians difficult.
segments.question: What effect would an American attack on Japan along the Aleutian chain have had on defenses elsewhere?
segments.answerShort: It was possible in theory, but currents, distance, cold, and the extra support burden made the Aleutian route much harder than the routes the Allies actually used.

segments.title: Evacuating Kiska through the American blockade
segments.body: American aircraft repeatedly bombed Kiska after its occupation. Fog later gave Japanese ships a way to penetrate the blockade and withdraw the garrison. Two light cruisers and ten destroyers evacuated 5,193 men. The same conditions that complicated operations in the Aleutians allowed the evacuation force to pass through waters under American pressure.

evidence.note: American bombing and the fog-covered evacuation of 5,193 men by two light cruisers and ten destroyers.

segments.summary: Fog allowed two Japanese light cruisers and ten destroyers to evacuate 5,193 men from Kiska through the blockade.

segments.title: Attu's civilians under occupation and in captivity
segments.body: Japanese troops occupied Attu in June 1942 and took the surviving inhabitants to Japan. Forty-two Aleuts survived the invasion and were sent to Hokkaido, where sixteen died in imprisonment. Radio operator Charles Jones had destroyed his radio and was killed after refusing to repair it. His wife Etta, a teacher and nurse, also entered captivity. After the war, surviving villagers moved to other islands because the Americans said they could not defend them on Attu. The village was never reoccupied.

evidence.note: The occupation, the 42 Aleuts sent to Hokkaido and sixteen deaths there, Charles Jones's destroyed radio, and Etta Jones's captivity.
Surviving villagers moved to other islands after the war, leaving Attu village unoccupied.

segments.summary: Attu's occupation brought civilian deaths, imprisonment in Japan, and permanent displacement of the surviving villagers.

segments.title: Attu's empty interval and costly American recapture
segments.body: Japan initially planned only a short occupation of Attu, and its first garrison shifted to Kiska. Attu was left empty from August until October 1942, an unnoticed interval that offered the possibility of a comparatively easy American recapture. Japan then returned in greater strength to build fortifications and an airfield. When 15,000 American troops landed in May 1943, nearly three weeks of fighting ended in a mass Japanese charge. American losses included 549 killed, more than 1,100 wounded, and thousands evacuated for weather-related injuries, while only 29 Japanese defenders survived. After the recapture, American forces built a better-sited airfield for bomber attacks against Japan.

evidence.note: Japan initially intended a short occupation of Attu, shifted the first garrison to Kiska, then returned in greater strength after leaving the island empty from August to October 1942.
The American landing, nearly three weeks of fighting, the final Japanese charge, heavy casualties, and construction of a new airfield.
Attu's empty interval offered a missed opportunity for a comparatively easy recapture before the Japanese returned.

segments.summary: An unnoticed interval without a Japanese garrison preceded the costly American landing on Attu in May 1943.

segments.title: Would 6,300 improved Zeros change the Pacific War?
segments.body: Authorized or projected aircraft numbers are different from usable force strength. Thousands of additional fighters could matter, but only if the industrial system produced them and the navy supplied fuel and trained aviators to fly them. A plan for 6,300 aircraft has military value only when production, logistics, and personnel arrive together. Without those supporting conditions, the paper total does not become combat power.

evidence.note: The proposed 6,300-fighter total would matter only if Japan could build, fuel, and fly the aircraft.

segments.summary: A projected force of 6,300 improved Zero fighters depended on actual production, fuel, and trained personnel.
segments.question: Would Japan's plan for 6,300 improved A6M8 Zero fighters have materially changed the war?
segments.answerShort: Yes, if Japan could actually build, fuel, crew, and operate them; the paper total alone could not create combat power.

segments.title: Kiska's evacuation and Operation Cottage
segments.body: Radio signals from Kiska ceased on July 28, bomb damage remained unrepaired, and aircrews reported greatly reduced anti-aircraft fire. These were signs of evacuation, yet American and Canadian troops landed on August 15 expecting resistance. The operation included the First Special Service Force's first deployment. Troops mistook one another for Japanese forces. Friendly fire killed 28 Americans and four Canadians, with 50 wounded on each side, while mines, booby traps, accidents, and unexploded hazards caused further casualties. A Japanese mine tore away part of USS Abner Read's stern, killing 71 and wounding 47. The abandoned island remained lethal without an enemy garrison present.

evidence.note: The booby-trapped island, the American and Canadian formations, and the evidence that Japanese forces had departed.
Although Japan had evacuated Kiska, friendly fire, mines, accidents, and other hazards caused Allied casualties, and a Japanese mine tore away part of USS Abner Read's stern.

segments.summary: Japan evacuated Kiska before the Allied landing, yet mines, booby traps, and friendly fire made Operation Cottage costly against an absent garrison.

segments.title: Radar uncertainty in the Battle of the Pips
segments.body: Task Group 16.22, centered on USS Mississippi and USS Idaho, opened fire on unexplained radar contacts in poor Aleutian weather. The battleships fired 518 fourteen-inch shells without hits or visual confirmation of Japanese warships. Brian Garfield proposed that the contacts were rafts of migratory seabirds. Japanese evacuation ships are another suggested possibility, although they were not thought to be within range. The identity of the contacts remains uncertain.

evidence.note: The 518-shell expenditure against uncertain contacts, Brian Garfield's seabird-raft theory, and the alternative possibility of Japanese evacuation ships despite doubts about their range.

segments.summary: Uncertain radar contacts prompted two American battleships to fire 518 fourteen-inch shells without a confirmed target or hit.

segments.title: Could a telephone cable explain Kiska's radio silence?
segments.body: Radio silence could have another explanation, including a switch to cable communications. The American blockade, however, would have made laying such a cable unusually difficult. It would have required a rapid operation by small fast ships or a submarine. Together with the other signs of evacuation, the loss of radio traffic warranted scouting flights before the landing.

evidence.note: The telephone-cable suggestion, the difficulty of installing one through the blockade, and the case for scouting flights.

segments.summary: The cable explanation for Kiska's radio silence raises a logistical problem and reinforces the case for reconnaissance.
segments.question: Could Kiska's radio silence have meant that the Japanese were using a telephone cable?
segments.answerShort: Installing a cable through the American blockade would itself have been an extraordinary engineering operation; the combined signs of evacuation warranted reconnaissance.

segments.title: How a war delayed to 1945 changes naval rearmament
segments.body: A 1945-start scenario gives Britain and the United States time to develop alongside Japan. Britain could have Lion-class battleships and more advanced carriers, while the United States enlarged its fleet and industrial base without wartime disruption. More 4.5-inch guns could produce British destroyers resembling the later Daring class through a different sequence of designs. Peacetime investment could also expand ship-support infrastructure in Australia, Canada, and India. The outcome would depend on competing investment choices and technical development, so Japanese aircraft upgrades cannot be considered in isolation.

evidence.note: Comparison of projected Japanese aircraft with British and American peacetime fleet and infrastructure development.
Additional 4.5-inch guns could produce a Daring-like standard British destroyer through a different development path.
Technical development depends on investment choices, with possible British infrastructure expansion in Australia, Canada, and India.

segments.summary: A war delayed to 1945 would allow competing fleet construction and infrastructure investment alongside Japan's aircraft development.
segments.question: If global war were delayed until 1945, would Japan's later carrier aircraft give it a decisive advantage?
segments.answerShort: Britain and the United States would also gain years to develop their fleets, industry, and overseas support infrastructure.

segments.title: Eric Brown's first carrier landing by a pure jet
segments.body: Eric Brown's December 1945 landing of a de Havilland Sea Vampire on HMS Ocean was the first carrier landing and takeoff by a fully jet-powered aircraft. The Ryan FR Fireball's earlier emergency arrival aboard USS Wake Island was different: the Fireball combined piston and jet power, was not landing under jet power, and crash-landed. Calling either event the first jet carrier landing without qualification hides those differences. Propulsion, intent, and whether the landing was controlled all matter when defining the record.

evidence.note: In December 1945, Eric Brown landed and took off from HMS Ocean in a fully jet-powered Sea Vampire.
The mixed piston-and-jet Ryan Fireball's emergency crash landing differed from Brown's controlled carrier landing in a pure jet.

segments.summary: The first jet carrier landing depends on whether the aircraft used pure or mixed power and whether its arrival was controlled.
segments.question: Who made the first carrier landing by a jet aircraft, and did the United States get there first?
segments.answerShort: Eric Brown made the first controlled carrier landing and takeoff by a pure jet in a Sea Vampire aboard HMS Ocean in December 1945, while the earlier American Ryan FR Fireball arrival was a crash landing by a mixed-power aircraft.

segments.title: Would Britain develop Centurion without wartime experience?
segments.body: A later war would not guarantee that Britain produced the same tanks on the historical timetable. Without combat experience, the Army might continue developing versions of its existing designs. Something like Centurion could emerge eventually, but the time required remains uncertain. The eventual borrowing of naval guns is raised as one possible part of that development.

evidence.note: The Centurion suggestion is qualified by the possibility of continued development of existing tanks without combat experience.
An eventual Centurion-like tank is considered possible, with uncertain timing and a comparison to Army use of naval guns.

segments.summary: Without wartime experience, British tank development could follow a different timetable even if something like Centurion eventually emerged.
segments.question: Would Britain have Centurion tanks if the war began later?
segments.answerShort: Possibly, but the Army might keep developing its existing tanks without wartime experience, so the timetable could differ.

segments.title: Yamato and British battleship retention in a delayed war
segments.body: In a war delayed until 1945, Japan could have three or four 18-inch-gun battleships, with Shinano remaining a battleship. Their armament would be difficult to conceal indefinitely and would prompt British and American responses. Older British ships would face different prospects: the Revenge class and unmodernized Queen Elizabeths would probably leave service, while other ships depended on replacement construction and modernization. Hood was a likely modernization candidate, and building Vanguards could reduce the case for retaining or rebuilding Repulse. Discovery of the Japanese ships would strengthen the argument for keeping Nelson and Rodney because of their armor, despite their limited speed. These are conditional fleet choices, not a historical modernization program.

evidence.note: A delayed war could leave several Japanese 18-inch-gun battleships in service, prompting British and American responses.
Conditional retention and modernization prospects for British capital ships, with Nelson and Rodney valued for armor despite low speed.

segments.summary: Discovery of Japan's 18-inch-gun battleships could change which British capital ships were retained or modernized before a later war.

segments.title: Could Japan have landed commandos from submarines?
segments.body: The Imperial Japanese Navy had long-range submarines and naval landing troops, but apparently did not combine them into an American coastal-raiding plan. Weak security at some coastal sites would have made sabotage raids possible. At Ellwood, landing troops to place charges could have caused more damage than shelling from offshore. One proposed propaganda tactic was to leave the personnel alive to report the raid and amplify its psychological effect. The resulting diversion of American money and troops toward coastal defense is judged capable of buying Japan at least another three or four months, a counterfactual estimate rather than a historical outcome.

evidence.note: Japanese submarine and landing-force capabilities, weak coastal security, a hypothetical sabotage raid at Ellwood, and the estimated diversion of American resources.

segments.summary: Japanese submarines and naval landing troops offered a hypothetical means of raiding coastal targets and diverting American resources into home defense.
segments.question: Did Japan plan submarine-carried commando raids against the United States?
segments.answerShort: Japan had both long-range submarines and naval landing troops, but it does not appear to have combined them into such a plan, even though the concept was feasible.
